'''Harold Hillman''' (16 August 1930 – 5 August 2016) was a British scientist and expert in the [[neurobiology]] of [[execution]] methods. He was born in London.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hq0EAAAAIAAJ&q=Harold+Hillman+1930+surrey |title = Who's Who of British Scientists 1980/81. 3rd ed|isbn = 9780862290016|year = 1980}}</ref><ref name=scientist>Richard Stevenson, [http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/9660/title/Good-Scientists--Bad-Science--Clinging-To-A--Dubious--Position-Can-Destroy-A-Career/ Good Scientists, Bad Science? Clinging To A 'Dubious' Position Can Destroy A Career], The Scientist, July 25, 1988</ref>

==Theories==
Hillman caused controversy in biological fields with his insistence that structures seen in cells under the [[electron microscope]] were little more than [[artifact (error)|artefacts]]. He maintained that up to 90 percent of the brain is made up of "a fine, granular material that is virtually liquid," and that the brain only has two cell types, instead of four.<ref>Hillman, 1996, p.71: "The greatest proportion of the central nervous system is a ground substance consisting of a fine granular material with ‘naked nuclei.’"</ref>

Mainstream scientists maintain that as fixation techniques have been compared with other analysis techniques, there is no explanation for why all the different techniques should produce identical artifacts.<ref name=scientist/>

Hillman's main field was neurobiology and [[resuscitation]], in which his work was largely uncontroversial.

==Charitable work==
Hillman was a founder member of [[Amnesty International]], and later produced research for the charity.<ref>{{cite news |title=Stun guns for police `can harm health' |date=23 June 2002 |work=The Independent }}</ref>

==Career==
Hillman was Reader in [[Physiology]] at the [[University of Surrey]] from 1965 until 1989, when he took early retirement after being threatened with loss of tenure. He wrote in 1996: "I believe that I am the only tenured academic in Britain who has lost his tenure because of his or her scientific views."<ref>Hillman, 1996, p.73</ref>

In 1997, he was awarded the [[Ig Nobel Prize|Ig Nobel Peace Prize]] for his report "The Possible Pain Experienced During Execution by Different Methods."<ref>{{Cite journal| last1 = Hiliman | first1 = H.| title = The possible pain experienced during execution by different methods| journal = Perception| volume = 22| issue = 6| pages = 745–821| year = 1993| doi = 10.1068/p220745| pmid = 8255703| s2cid = 28706073}}</ref>

Harold Hillman died peacefully of [[heart failure]] on 5 August 2016. He was survived by his wife, their children, and their grandchildren.<ref>[http://www.bmdsonline.co.uk/surrey-herald-chertsey-addlestone-byfleet-&-woking/obituary/hillman-dr/47783972?s_source=tmso_bmd_sca Hillman, Dr.: Obituary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828221457/http://www.bmdsonline.co.uk/surrey-herald-chertsey-addlestone-byfleet-%26-woking/obituary/hillman-dr/47783972?s_source=tmso_bmd_sca |date=28 August 2016 }}, Surrey Herald</ref>

==Personal life==
Hillman was born to [[David Hillman (artist)]], a well known producer of stained glass, who was the son of Rabbi [[Shmuel Yitzchak Hillman]].<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oC1KDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT146 | title=The Jewish Journey: A Passage through European History| isbn=9780857739780| last1=Gelles| first1=Edward| date=2015-11-26}}</ref> His brothers were [[Ellis Hillman]] and [[Mayer Hillman]], and he was a cousin of [[Chaim Herzog]], the sixth President of Israel and father of [[Isaac Herzog|Issac Herzo]]<nowiki/>g, the current president of Israel.
